dailyBrief.text: Good morning — the warm spell is over: Solon turns partly cloudy and much cooler today, high near 56° after yesterday's 76°, with a chilly low around 38° tonight. Overnight, Iran said four oil tankers hit mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after the U.S. said the main lanes were cleared, and Binance disclosed a $6.3 billion hack, the biggest theft in crypto history. The Cavs rallied late but fell 114-111 at Atlanta — Harden had 24 and Mitchell 22 — and they're back at it Halloween night in Milwaukee. Today locally, early in-person voting runs 7:30 AM to 7:30 PM, Jurassic Quest opens downtown, and Pumpkins & Piranhas has its final night at the aquarium.

The standout deal is still Giant Eagle's BOGO-free sirloin tip roasts through November 4 — and with the baby due in early November, this is officially any-day-now week.

Tanker hit by limpet mines in the Strait of Hormuz as Iran says it stopped two more ships
items.summary:
A small boat placed two limpet mines on the hull of a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, setting off a fire in the ship's engine room and disabling it for a time, maritime security sources told Reuters on Friday. The crew was safe, the fire was put out, there was no environmental damage, and the Panama-flagged vessel was able to continue to its next port, according to the British navy's UK Maritime Trade Operations agency. The attack happened about 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman.

It was the first successful use of limpet mines in the waterway since the U.S. war with Iran began in February, the sources said, after a similar attempt in September failed to detonate. Separately on Friday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards navy said two more oil tankers had been involved in incidents and stopped south of the strait after ignoring radio warnings and trying an unauthorized route, and Tehran also claimed its forces destroyed a U.S. unmanned boat east of the strait — a claim the U.S. military did not immediately confirm.

The strait is one of the world's most important energy chokepoints, carrying roughly a fifth of global oil and gas shipments, so every attack there rattles energy markets and raises the risk of a wider clash. The mine attack landed a day after Washington said the main shipping lanes had been cleared, undercutting that message.

Qatari mediators were reported back in Tehran on Friday for another round of talks aimed at ending the war. Watch whether shipping companies pause transits again and whether the mediation produces any pause in the attacks.

items.title: Rare Russia-Ukraine truce lets aid convoy reach the devastated city of Oleshky
items.summary:
A humanitarian mission entered the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine on Friday, on the fourth day of a local ceasefire that officials called the most significant truce of the four-and-a-half-year war. A convoy of 25 buses, ambulances and aid supplies brought food and medicine into the city and began evacuating residents who want to leave for Russia or for Ukrainian-controlled territory. About 2,000 people are still living in Oleshky.

The ceasefire in the Kherson region has held since Tuesday and is due to run through Sunday evening. Routes into the city were demined late Thursday, work in which two people were killed. Russia and Ukraine issued identical statements promising that everyone who wishes to leave can do so safely and that those who stay will receive humanitarian support. The White House said first lady Melania Trump helped broker the pause, and Pope Leo XIV also pressed both sides to allow the mission.

The operation is a rare moment of direct cooperation between the two governments in a war otherwise defined by attrition — fighting continued elsewhere, with both sides reporting large overnight drone and missile attacks outside the truce zone.

Evacuees heading to Ukraine face a long route through Russia and Belarus and were expected to arrive Saturday. The test ahead is whether the pause ends on schedule Sunday or becomes a template for similar local arrangements.

items.title: Spain's transport minister rejects resignation calls as train-crash toll reaches 69
items.summary:
Spain's transport minister, Óscar Puente, on Friday rejected calls to resign over Wednesday's high-speed train collision near Urda, in Toledo province, which has now killed at least 69 people. A state-run Renfe train travelling at an estimated 160 to 200 kilometres per hour struck the rear of a stationary Iryo train on the Madrid–Seville line, derailing carriages. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the crash site on Friday as recovery and victim-identification work continued.

A preliminary account points to a chain of failures: a malfunction knocked out the line's LZB train-protection system over roughly 63 kilometres, trains were stopped automatically, and Madrid's central control centre then authorized the Renfe train to proceed even though the Iryo train was still ahead of it. The Renfe service was carrying 379 passengers and seven crew; the Iryo train had 147 passengers and five crew.

Puente has blamed a serious error of judgment by a traffic controller, but rail unions say that framing is unfair and point to staffing shortages, workloads and the failed signalling system. The disaster is Spain's deadliest rail accident since 2013 and the second mass-casualty crash on the same line this year, after January's Adamuz collision killed 46 people.

Puente is due to address Congress on November 3. Investigators have not yet confirmed the exact speed or a final cause, and attention is turning to compensation for victims' families and to whether the line's safety systems get an overhaul.

items.title: G20 ministers scrap their group photo in Atlanta after Europeans refuse to pose with Russia's Lavrov
items.summary:
The G20 foreign ministers' meeting opened in Atlanta on Friday without its traditional group photo, after more than a third of the delegations — including European countries, Canada and Australia — said they would not be pictured alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the host, cancelled the photo altogether, with U.S. officials saying they did not want a ceremonial moment to become a spectacle that overshadowed the talks.

In his opening remarks, Rubio urged the ministers to work together for geopolitical stability and economic prosperity, warning that a series of crises threatens the global economic order. Germany's foreign minister said there could be no photo with Lavrov because there is 'no normalcy with Russia,' and Britain cited its longstanding policy against direct engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine. Canada's foreign minister missed the opening session, South Africa was not invited by the U.S. presidency, and Ukraine was not invited either.

The standoff shows how far apart Washington and many of its allies remain on Russia, even as the Trump administration keeps channels to Moscow open. The two-day meeting is meant to lay the groundwork for a G20 leaders' summit President Trump will host at his Miami golf club in December.

Watch whether the ministers can agree on any joint language about Ukraine and the Middle East this weekend, or whether the Atlanta meeting ends without a common statement.

items.title: Israel's final results leave no winner, and Netanyahu's fraud claims draw a backlash
items.summary:
Final results from this week's Israeli election confirm a deadlock: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot won 48, both short of the 61 needed to govern. The two Arab-led lists, the Joint List and Ra'am, won a record 19 seats after turnout in some Arab localities surged toward 80 percent, making them potential kingmakers.

Netanyahu and his Likud party have alleged, without presenting evidence, that the Arab parties 'stole' the election through bribery and foreign interference, and the head of the Central Elections Committee asked the Shin Bet security agency to investigate claims of Qatari and Turkish funding. The committee's acting director general said there was no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity, Qatar rejected the claims as ridiculous and dangerous, and Ra'am's leader said his party had no connection to the affair and would cooperate with investigators.

Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of running an orchestrated campaign to delegitimize the results, and Arab leaders called the allegations incitement. Analysts say the pressure may be aimed less at overturning the count than at making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Arab support from outside the coalition.

Weeks of coalition negotiations lie ahead. The Shin Bet inquiry and whether any bloc can assemble 61 seats — or Israel heads toward yet another election — are the stories to watch.

items.title: Italian peacekeeping helicopter crash kills four in Bosnia as UN renews the EU mission
items.summary:
Four Italian personnel were killed and 11 injured when an Italian Army CH-47 Chinook helicopter crashed during a routine training flight near Gorice, in Bosnia's Brčko District, on Thursday evening. All 15 people aboard were Italian: the dead were two army soldiers and two members of the Italian Red Cross military volunteer corps. The injured were treated in Brčko and Tuzla and were reported stable, and no civilians were hurt.

The helicopter was flying for EUFOR Althea, the European Union's peacekeeping operation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Brčko declared Friday a day of mourning, Italy's prime minister Giorgia Meloni expressed grief over the deaths, and the Italian defence minister travelled to visit the wounded. Both EUFOR and Italy's defence ministry have opened investigations; no cause has been announced.

In a separate Friday development, the UN Security Council voted unanimously to extend EUFOR Althea's authorization for another year, and council members expressed condolences over the crash during the session.

Investigators will be looking at what brought down a large, twin-rotor transport helicopter on a routine flight in good circumstances. EUFOR says it will release verified findings as the inquiry progresses.

items.title: Appeals court again refuses to let the Justice Department set aside 20,000 California ballots
items.summary:
A federal appeals court on Friday rejected the Trump administration's emergency request to block California from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters the Justice Department alleges are likely noncitizens. The 2-1 ruling by a 9th Circuit panel was the administration's second loss in the case this week, four days before the November 3 midterms, and it leaves the disputed ballots in the normal count.

The majority — Judges Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, and Gabriel Sanchez, a Biden appointee — pointed to the district court's finding that the administration's list may not be fully reliable and wrote that there is a material risk the requested order would disenfranchise lawful voters. Judge Patrick Bumatay dissented. District Judge David Carter had denied the original request on Wednesday, saying it would wreak havoc on an election already underway; California says about one in four voters on the list was born in the United States.

The Justice Department sued California on October 15, after mail ballots had already gone out, demanding the state segregate the listed voters' ballots until citizenship could be verified. State and county officials said ballots already processed have been separated from their envelopes, making reliable matching effectively impossible.

The department could still ask the full 9th Circuit or the Supreme Court to intervene, but it has not said whether it will. Counties keep counting in the meantime, with certification deadlines in December.

items.title: Trump puts his Kansas and Iowa rallies back on for Sunday after cancelling them a day earlier
items.summary:
President Trump reversed course on Friday and restored the two in-person rallies he had abruptly cancelled a day earlier, saying he will campaign in Kansas and Iowa back-to-back on Sunday, November 1, two days before the midterms. He told reporters in the Oval Office that Republicans in both states called and asked him to come in person rather than appear by tele-rally.

The original plan had Trump skipping the weekend trips — Saturday in Salina, Kansas, for Sen. Roger Marshall and Sunday in Dubuque, Iowa, for Rep. Ashley Hinson — in favour of more than 20 tele-rallies across many states. The White House now says he will do both: nearly 20 tele-rallies plus the two restored in-person events. Trump held a rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday and has held more than two dozen rallies in the campaign's homestretch.

The whiplash underlined how tight the map has become: a CNN/SSRS poll of Kansas likely voters conducted October 20-26 put Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton ahead of Marshall 49 to 45 percent in a state Republicans usually hold comfortably.

Watch Sunday's turnout and tone in both states — and whether the late schedule change moves anything in two Senate races Republicans expected to bank.

items.title: Pentagon's top planner is removed as a leak investigation and Iran options reach the president
items.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has removed Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, the Joint Staff's director for strategy, plans and policy — the Pentagon's chief planner — amid allegations that he leaked classified information about the wars in Ukraine and Iran to reporters. An internal investigative report says Sylvia admitted leaking classified material to two reporters from different outlets over the course of a year, and the case has been referred for possible prosecution.

The removal lands at a sensitive moment. Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, briefed President Trump in person this week on military options for the Iran war, according to the Wall Street Journal, and Trump has teased returning to military action after Tuesday's midterms. On Friday the president publicly backed Hegseth's decision, sharing posts from commentators praising the firing.

Two Pentagon sources have disputed parts of the official account to CBS News, raising questions about whether this was a straightforward security case or something more political. Either way, the office responsible for the military's most sensitive strategic planning has lost its leader days before an election that could decide the war's next phase.

What to watch: whether charges follow, who replaces Sylvia, and whether the administration acts on the Iran options Cooper presented once the voting is over.

items.title: Alaska's governor orders an investigation of Mary Peltola's campaign and floats withholding Senate certification
items.summary:
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered the state's Department of Public Safety to investigate Democrat Mary Peltola's Senate campaign, following accusations that it helped recruit a little-known candidate named Dan J. Sullivan to run in order to confuse voters — because the incumbent Republican senator is named Dan S. Sullivan. Dunleavy suggested any finding of illegal conduct could affect whether the winner is seated, raising the possibility that the state might withhold certification of the Senate result.

Vice President JD Vance, asked this week, did not say whether he agreed with President Trump's call to prosecute Peltola. The dispute has turned an already unusual same-name ballot situation into a national fight over who gets to decide a Senate race: voters, or state officials after the fact.

Election lawyers note that seating senators is ultimately the Senate's own constitutional call, and that withholding state certification would invite an immediate court fight. Peltola's campaign has denied wrongdoing.

The race is close enough that the investigation itself is now a campaign issue. Watch for any findings before Tuesday — and for how Senate leaders in Washington respond if Alaska's result is challenged.

items.title: Young men who powered Trump's 2024 win are souring on Republicans ahead of the midterms
items.summary:
Young men, one of the groups that swung hardest to Donald Trump in 2024, are drifting away from Republicans days before the midterms, according to a YouGov/Economist poll conducted October 23-26. Trump's approval among young men has fallen from 54 percent at the start of his term to 38 percent, with 57 percent now disapproving.

The shift matters because of how recently the ground moved: validated-voter studies showed young men backing Trump by about six points in 2024, and men under 30 by about twelve — a realignment both parties treated as durable. Pollsters and campaign analysts say cost-of-living frustration is doing much of the damage, and some of these voters say they may simply stay home rather than switch parties.

Democrats are not automatically winning the group back; the polling describes reconsideration and abstention more than conversion. But in a midterm decided by turnout, a few points of enthusiasm lost in a core constituency can flip close House and Senate races.

Tuesday's exit polls will show whether the drift was real. Campaigns are watching young men's turnout in the Kansas, Iowa and Alaska Senate races especially closely.

items.title: A flood of partisan polls is clouding the final midterm picture, forecasters warn
items.summary:
Election forecasters are warning voters to treat the last wave of midterm polling with skepticism. Partisan and incentivized polls — some commissioned to generate a favourable headline rather than to measure the race — are being amplified on social media, where a single eye-catching number can travel further than a careful average.

The Hill's Decision Desk HQ averages still show a generic congressional ballot that is close to tied, with control of Congress likely to hinge on a small number of House districts and about four competitive Senate states. Experts quoted this week stressed a different problem as well: even honest polls can systematically miss certain kinds of voters, and herding around a consensus number can hide real movement.

The practical effect is a fog over the final weekend. Campaigns are making closing decisions — where to send the president, where to buy the last ads — with less reliable information than the volume of numbers suggests.

The safest read remains the averages and the highest-quality public polls, not individual releases. Tuesday night's results will also serve as a verdict on which pollsters' methods actually found the electorate.

items.title: Stocks close sharply lower as the AI trade unravels; Nasdaq suffers its worst month since March 2025
items.summary:
Wall Street ended October with a steep sell-off on Friday as investors bailed out of the artificial-intelligence trade. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 2.9 percent to 25,437, the S&P 500 lost about 1.8 percent to 7,580, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped about 1.1 percent to 51,770 — a second straight down day after Thursday's Alphabet-driven slide. The technology sector was the day's biggest loser, while energy, staples, utilities and health care held up better.

Intel was the emblem of the rout, plunging roughly 29 percent in its worst session since 1974 after a weak outlook (see the separate story below). Amazon also fell after its earnings, bitcoin slid below $77,000 in the wake of the Binance hack, and gold touched a one-year low. The Nasdaq finished October down more than 5 percent, its worst month since March 2025, and now sits more than 8 percent below its October 6 record close; one Reuters estimate put the Nasdaq 100 on track to shed more than $2 trillion in market value for the month. The Dow, by contrast, gained ground in October.

Beneath the wreckage, earnings season itself has been solid: of the 299 S&P 500 companies that had reported third-quarter results by Friday, about 82 percent beat expectations, according to LSEG data. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 4.93 percent.

Next week brings the October manufacturing and services surveys and a run of jobs data, including the monthly payrolls report — the first clean test of whether this was an AI-valuation reset or the start of something broader.

items.title: Intel plunges about 29% in its worst day since 1974 after a weak outlook
items.summary:
Intel shares collapsed roughly 29 percent on Friday, closing near $66 in the stock's worst day since 1974, after the chipmaker paired decent third-quarter numbers with a fourth-quarter outlook that missed Wall Street's expectations. One estimate put the day's loss at around $150 billion in market value.

The quarter itself beat forecasts: revenue of about $15.1 billion and adjusted earnings of 29 cents a share both topped estimates, and the data-center and AI segment grew about 22 percent to roughly $5.4 billion. The problem was the PC business, where revenue fell about 5 percent to roughly $7.7 billion, and guidance for fourth-quarter revenue of $12.2 to $13.2 billion came in below the roughly $12.9 billion analysts expected. Intel's finance chief pointed to restructuring costs, soft consumer demand and intensifying competition.

The split result captures Intel's larger dilemma: its AI data-center business is growing, but the legacy PC engine that funds the turnaround is shrinking, and CEO Lip-Bu Tan is reviewing the company's costly foundry ambitions.

Analysts will be watching whether the foundry review produces asset sales or partnerships — and whether Friday's reset makes Intel a value story or a value trap.

items.title: Binance sets aside $6.34 billion to cover the record hack and aims to restart withdrawals before Sunday
items.summary:
Binance said Friday it has reserved more than $6.34 billion of company money to make customers whole after Thursday's theft of an estimated $6.3 billion from its hot wallets — the largest crypto hack on record. About $5 billion of the reserve is already held in the exact tokens that were taken, and roughly $3 billion of the stolen assets have been frozen with help from industry partners.

Withdrawals remain paused while Binance rebuilds its withdrawal service and rotates addresses; co-CEO Richard Teng said the exchange aims to restart them within about 40 to 48 hours, ahead of a Sunday, November 1 deadline, and only after rigorous testing. Deposits are operating normally, Binance.US says it was unaffected, and the company plans to publish a full proof-of-reserves report by Monday, November 2. The exchange first blamed a compromised engineer's laptop and later said investigators had found additional points of breach.

The fallout rippled through crypto finance: lending protocol Aave briefly blocked new deposits and borrowing after an attacker borrowed ether against stolen tokens, then reopened Friday with nine assets barred as collateral for new loans. TRM Labs estimates the attacker still controls about $2.4 billion in bitcoin and ether beyond any issuer's reach, and analysts at Chainalysis, TRM and Elliptic link the theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor group.

The weekend test is mechanical and reputational at once: withdrawals reopening on schedule, and a proof-of-reserves report that convinces customers the money is really there.

items.title: Polymarket says a vendor's compromised code drained $2.7 million from 737 accounts
items.summary:
Prediction-market platform Polymarket lost about $2.7 million on Thursday when malicious code slipped into its systems through DebugBear, a third-party website-monitoring vendor, and was used to drain funds from 737 user accounts over roughly four hours. The company says no attacker broke its core systems or cryptography; the breach came through the vendor's code.

Polymarket paused parts of the platform for about five hours, blocked new deposits during the pause, and has promised to reimburse every affected user in full, in USDC. Trading operations have since resumed.

Coming on the same day as the $6.3 billion Binance theft, the incident underlines a pattern in modern crypto breaches: the target is rarely the blockchain itself but the ordinary software and suppliers around it — an engineer's laptop in Binance's case, a monitoring script in Polymarket's.

Watch for the company's post-mortem and whether it changes how prediction markets vet third-party code, especially with election-week betting volumes running high.

items.title: Alphabet slides as a cloud miss and a bigger AI spending bill rattle investors
items.summary:
Alphabet shares fell sharply this week after the Google parent reported third-quarter results that beat on the top line but disappointed where it counted most: the cloud. Revenue rose about 13 percent to roughly $118 billion and net income reached about $44.8 billion, helped by a large unrealized gain on the company's SpaceX stake — but Google Cloud revenue of about $18.8 billion, up 27 percent, missed the roughly $19.5 billion analysts expected, its first cloud miss in six quarters.

Management also raised this year's capital-spending plans to between $180 and $190 billion, most of it for AI data centers and servers, and YouTube advertising revenue of about $10.9 billion came in light as well. One bright spot was Waymo, where paid rides grew roughly 37 percent from the prior quarter.

The reaction summed up the market's new mood: investors who once rewarded any AI spending announcement are now asking what the spending earns. Alphabet's slide on Thursday helped pull the whole technology sector into Friday's broader sell-off.

The question for the next quarter is whether cloud growth re-accelerates before the spending does. Alphabet's answer will likely set the tone for every other AI builder's stock.

items.title: Gold sinks to a new low for the year as Federal Reserve hawks talk about more rate hikes
items.summary:
Gold fell more than 3 percent on Friday to around $3,884 an ounce, breaking below $3,900 for the first time in a year, as hawkish comments from Federal Reserve officials collided with a strong economy. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan called for two more rate hikes, and St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem argued for another hike soon.

The backdrop helps explain the pressure: U.S. economic growth ran at a healthy 3.4 percent year-over-year pace in the third quarter, well above forecasts, giving the Fed little reason to ease. Gold, which pays no yield, tends to suffer when rates look set to stay higher for longer — even on a day when stock markets were falling sharply.

The move caps a reversal for one of the year's most crowded trades. Investors who bought gold as protection against market turmoil watched it fall alongside stocks on Friday, a reminder that it hedges some risks and not others.

Next week's calendar is packed — manufacturing and services surveys, job openings, ADP employment, jobless claims and the monthly payrolls report — and any of them could move the rate debate, and gold with it.

items.title: Record king tides flood both coasts, closing highways and pushing water into homes
items.summary:
Exceptionally high king tides flooded coastal communities from Southern California to South Florida this week, closing a stretch of Pacific Coast Highway near Huntington Beach, sending seawater into streets, homes and businesses, and setting water-level records on both coasts. A San Diego tide gauge topped 8 feet, nearly a foot and a half above prediction, and Los Angeles Harbor set records on consecutive days; experts said some Southern California gauges logged their highest coastal water levels in more than a century of records.

Florida saw its own records: Virginia Key recorded its highest king tide and third-highest water level in roughly 30 years, and water at South Port Everglades reached about 2.25 feet above ground, topping a mark set during Hurricane Nicole in 2022. Huntington Beach's city council met Friday to ratify a local emergency proclaimed earlier in the week.

King tides occur when the sun and moon align and the moon is near its closest point to Earth; this round coincided with the full Hunter's moon and was amplified by warmer ocean water linked to El Niño and, in Florida, persistent onshore winds. No storm was involved — the flooding arrived under clear skies.

Forecasters expect the water to ease as the peak tides pass, though rough surf and erosion risks linger into early next week. The next scheduled king-tide windows fall during Thanksgiving week and again around Christmas, and scientists warn those could run higher still.

items.title: Colleges race to teach the influencer economy as content creation becomes a career track
items.summary:
Universities are building degree programs, majors and certificates around content creation, racing to formalize a job path that a generation of students is already pursuing on phones and laptops. Programs highlighted this week include creative-industries and creator-focused tracks at schools such as Northeastern, Arizona State, Syracuse and Georgia, with at least one university planning a dedicated influencer-marketing major.

The money explains the rush: analysts estimate the global creator economy in the hundreds of billions of dollars, and brands increasingly hire graduates who understand audiences, platforms and analytics as well as cameras. Schools say employer demand is real — agencies, media companies and consumer brands all recruit for roles that did not exist a decade ago.

Skeptics ask whether a degree can teach the taste and timing that make creators succeed, and whether programs built around today's platforms will age well as platforms change. Faculty counter that the durable skills — storytelling, business, law and data — outlast any single app.

Enrollment numbers over the next two admission cycles will show whether students treat these programs as a serious credential or a novelty. Either way, the creator economy now has a syllabus.

items.title: Death of the judge in the social-media surveillance case leaves the immigrants' lawsuit in limbo
items.summary:
The federal judge overseeing a major challenge to the government's monitoring of immigrants' social media has died, throwing the case's future into uncertainty days before the midterms. Judge Charles Breyer of the Northern District of California, who was 84, had ruled in 2025 against the State Department's collection of social media handles from visa applicants and immigrants.

The government appealed that ruling, and Breyer's death means the appellate panel handling the case will have to be reconstituted or the matter reassigned — a process that could delay a decision well past the election. The case tests how far the government may go in screening people's online speech and associations as part of immigration enforcement.

Civil-liberties groups backing the challenge say the surveillance chills lawful speech; the administration argues the checks are a legitimate security tool. Both sides now face a longer wait, and possibly a different judicial audience, than either expected.

Watch for the appeals court's scheduling order, which will signal whether the case speeds up under a new judge or drifts into next year.

items.title: Fake anti-trans texts and mailers in Texas are traced to a Florida firm, investigation finds
items.summary:
Voters in competitive Texas districts have been receiving text messages and mailers from a group calling itself 'Defend Our Kids Texas,' attacking candidates over transgender issues — and a KXAN investigation has traced the operation to a Florida firm with ties to a Texas prison contractor. The senders behind the messages had not been publicly identified until the reporting this week.

The mailers arrived in the final stretch before Tuesday's midterms, in races where small margins could decide control of the statehouse and affect the congressional map. Texas campaign-finance and communications rules require disclosure of who pays for election messaging, and the group's structure appeared designed to obscure that.

Election officials remind voters that unsolicited texts about candidates are campaign material, not official information, and should be checked against trusted sources. The revelation also adds Texas to the list of states where outside money and murky groups are shaping the last weekend of the campaign.

What happens next depends on whether regulators or opposing campaigns file complaints — and whether voters in the targeted districts punish or reward the tactic on Tuesday.

items.title: Hegseth's Pentagon tenure faces its hardest week, with Trump tensions and the Iran war closing in
items.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is ending the week at the center of three storms at once: the removal of the Pentagon's top planner over alleged leaks, bipartisan criticism of his leadership, and open tension with President Trump over the conduct of the war in Iran. Profiles published this week describe a secretary whose future is being openly questioned in Washington even as he retains his job.

The immediate flashpoint was Thursday's firing of the Joint Staff's J5 director, which the administration framed as a security matter and critics framed as a purge. Behind it sits a larger argument about strategy: the president has teased renewed military action against Iran after the midterms, and the Pentagon's planning leadership turned over at exactly the moment those options were being briefed to him.

Hegseth's defenders say he is enforcing discipline in a building that leaks; his critics, now including voices in both parties, say the department is losing experienced planners faster than it can replace them.

Tuesday's election may decide the timeline. A result that strengthens the president's hand could settle Hegseth's position either way — confirmed as the enforcer, or moved aside once the voting is done.

items.title: Acton and Ramaswamy make their final pitches in a bruising Ohio governor's race
items.summary:
Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy are crisscrossing Ohio in the final days of a governor's race that made national headlines for its nastiness. Acton, who served as Gov. Mike DeWine's health director during the pandemic, is promising to break decades of Republican control of state government, fully fund public schools and cut taxes for working Ohioans. Ramaswamy, backed by President Trump, is pitching the elimination of the state income tax, property-tax rollbacks, a review of how Ohio runs its universities and an end to sanctuary cities.

The race turned uglier over a Ramaswamy attack ad focused on Acton's personal history. A Republican memo obtained by Axios said the ad was having a significant effect on the race, a Suffolk University–USA Today poll found Ramaswamy's favourability had dropped, and by Thursday the ad was no longer running on Ohio airwaves. Ramaswamy has spent $41.3 million of his own money on the campaign, including more than $1 million on private-jet travel, according to newly released finance reports. In the final stretch, both candidates backed temporarily eliminating the state gas tax, and Republicans passed a 90-day suspension.

The closing argument played out on big stages: Trump rallied in Chillicothe on Wednesday, and Acton answered from Cleveland Public Auditorium at a rally headlined by former President Barack Obama — his first Ohio campaign stop in eight years.

Early in-person voting runs Saturday 8 AM to 4 PM and ends Sunday 1 to 5 PM, with Election Day on Tuesday, November 3. Expect this one to be counted late into the night.

items.title: Massive Euclid warehouse fire draws 19 departments and about 110 firefighters overnight
items.summary:
Firefighters from 19 departments — about 110 people in all — battled a massive warehouse fire in Euclid that was reported late Thursday night and burned into Friday. The fire, near East 222nd Street and Tungsten Avenue, sent up exploding propane tanks as crews worked, and the building was destroyed.

Remarkably, no injuries were reported. Lakeshore Boulevard (Route 20) was closed while crews worked, the Red Cross responded to help, and investigators had not identified a cause by Friday afternoon. Fire officials said the effort focused on keeping the fire from spreading to neighbouring industrial buildings.

A multi-alarm industrial fire of this size is a regional event: mutual-aid crews came from across eastern Cuyahoga County and beyond, and residents across Euclid woke to smoke and road closures on Friday morning.

Watch for the fire marshal's cause determination and for any environmental checks on runoff and air quality around the site over the weekend.

items.title: Cleveland City Council's $5 million summer safety plan stalls in committee, 4-5
items.summary:
A $5 million proposal to fund summer safety in Cleveland — built mostly around police overtime — failed to advance out of a City Council committee this week on a 4-to-5 vote, leaving the plan short of a floor vote for now. The package included about $3.8 million for police overtime, roughly $223,000 for safety cameras and about $75,000 for drones.

The arithmetic was unusual: the committee's safety chair recused himself because his son is a Cleveland police officer, and three members who supported the plan were absent, so a proposal with majority backing on paper could not get out of committee. The debate split along familiar lines — supporters arguing the city must fund visible safety, skeptics questioning overtime spending and objecting to the camera and drone components. One absent supporter said she would have voted yes.

The vote comes weeks after an October 18 shooting near Shaker Square killed one person and wounded seven others, including a 12-year-old, which sharpened the city's argument over how to spend safety money.

Supporters can try to revive the plan in a later session. Watch whether the mayor's office pushes for a special vote — and whether the camera and drone money gets stripped to win over skeptics.

items.title: Browns' final injury report: Howard questionable, Dawand Jones in line to face T.J. Watt, and Sanders confirmed as QB2
items.summary:
Cleveland wrapped up its week of practice in Berea on Friday with one big question left for Sunday's first-place showdown in Pittsburgh: starting right tackle Tytus Howard, who suffered a concussion last week, did not practice at all this week and is officially questionable. Head coach Todd Monken said a decision will likely come Saturday; if Howard cannot go, Dawand Jones starts at right tackle — across from Steelers star T.J. Watt. Cornerback Myles Harden (hamstring) and safety Daniel Thomas (ankle) are also questionable.

The rest of Friday's news was good. Defensive tackle Mason Graham was removed from the report, edge rusher Jared Verse (knee) is off the report and a full go, and running back Dylan Sampson practiced fully Friday and was cleared after a knee issue. Monken also settled the quarterback room on Friday: Shedeur Sanders remains the backup behind Deshaun Watson, with Dillon Gabriel and Taylen Green still competing for the emergency third spot.

Both teams are 5-2, and sole possession of first place in the AFC North is on the line Sunday at 1 PM on CBS at Acrisure Stadium. Cleveland won the first meeting 27-24 in Week 4, but the Browns have lost 22 straight regular-season games in Pittsburgh — a streak dating back two decades, with their January 2021 playoff win the lone exception.

Saturday's call on Howard is the last piece. Jones, who admitted he 'did a bad job' filling in against the Jets last month, would be making the highest-leverage start of his season.

items.title: Ohio State heads to USC on Halloween night with a freshman in line to start at quarterback
items.summary:
No. 3 Ohio State (6-1) plays at No. 16 USC (6-1) on Saturday night at 7:30 PM ET on NBC at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum — and the Buckeyes will do it without starting quarterback Julian Sayin, who hurt his throwing shoulder in the fourth quarter of the 19-15 win at Indiana and is out indefinitely. Coach Ryan Day has said the team is planning as if Sayin could miss the rest of the season.

True freshman Luke Fahey, a Southern California native who replaced Sayin at Indiana, is in line to make his first start back home. Day has declined to formally name a starter and says fellow freshman Tavien St. Clair has also taken first-team reps and will be ready; reports this week named Fahey the starter. Whoever plays has the country's best safety net: receiver Jeremiah Smith, with more than 900 yards and 11 touchdowns this season.

USC averages in the mid-30s in points per game, but its pass defence has been vulnerable, and Ohio State's defence is the Buckeyes' argument that a freshman quarterback only has to be steady, not spectacular. Oddsmakers have Ohio State favoured by roughly a touchdown. One oddity for the notebook: Ohio State has not won a regular-season game at USC since 1946.

Kickoff is 7:30 PM Saturday on NBC. The first quarter — and how Day handles the quarterback if Fahey struggles early — will tell most of the story.

items.title: Cavs look to bounce back on Halloween night in Milwaukee after a late rally fell short in Atlanta
items.summary:
Cleveland's three-game winning streak ended Thursday night in Atlanta, where the Hawks held off a late Cavaliers rally for a 114-111 win. Atlanta led by ten with under five minutes left, but Cleveland twice cut it to one — the second time on a Donovan Mitchell basket with 21 seconds remaining — before Nickeil Alexander-Walker's free throws with 15.3 seconds left sealed it. Onyeka Okongwu led Atlanta with a season-high 29 points and 12 rebounds.

James Harden paced the Cavs with a season-high 24 points, Mitchell added 22, and Sam Merrill scored 16 off the bench with four three-pointers. The loss dropped Cleveland to 3-2, sixth in the East.

The Cavs get no rest: they play Saturday night at 8 PM ET at Milwaukee's Fiserv Forum. The Bucks are 1-4 in their first season of a post-Giannis Antetokounmpo rebuild, led by Tyler Herro's 23.4 points per game; Mitchell leads Cleveland at 24.2 per game. Cleveland guard Meleek Thomas is out with a foot injury.

After Milwaukee, the Cavs come home to host Oklahoma City on Monday — a two-game swing that will say a lot about how this veteran group handles its first back-to-back test of the season.

baby.tip: Dress-rehearse the hospital run: drive the route once together, note where to park and where to check in after hours, and keep the car topped up with fuel. With the car-seat base already installed, one calm practice trip now means the real one is just a drive, not a scramble.
baby.fact: A newborn's stomach is tiny at first — about the size of a cherry on day one and a walnut by day three — which is exactly why little-and-often feeds are the plan at the start. That small capacity grows fast over the first month.
